rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A moderate temperature leaves room to probe temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Change only gradient duration to identify slope-sensitive critical pairs, especially the late co-elution. This diagnostic run will show whether a shallower gradient improves selectivity enough to justify trimming the solvent window afterward.

The late co-elution barely responds to gradient slope, so test temperature-dependent selectivity against injection 1. Higher temperature should also create time headroom for subsequent resolution improvements.

Test the low-temperature endpoint because heating worsened several critical pairs without separating the late co-elution. Keeping the gradient unchanged isolates the temperature effect and should leave the last peak close to 10 minutes.

Raise the starting organic fraction to remove low-organic waiting time while making the gradient shallower at the best temperature tested. This should spread slope-sensitive late pairs and probe whether a different solvent window separates the persistent co-elution.

Use the time headroom from injection 5 to test a shallower gradient without changing the solvent window. This should improve the middle and late slope-sensitive pairs while keeping the last peak near 10 minutes.

Shift the starting fraction upward to shorten retention while further reducing gradient steepness. The earliest peaks still have retention margin, and the shallower slope may improve the remaining late pairs without exceeding 10 minutes.

Use an intermediate starting fraction to preserve early-pair resolution while retaining the shallower slope of injection 7. The last peak should remain near 10 minutes, with better separation of the middle critical pairs than at phi0 0.35.

Test temperature selectivity at the best-performing gradient slope, since temperature effects may differ from the initial steeper gradient. This also measures whether faster elution creates useful room for further slope reduction.

Probe a lower final organic fraction so the difficult late cluster elutes near the gradient-to-hold transition, testing selectivity not accessed by slope or temperature changes so far. The stronger start and short gradient limit the time cost, though the final peak may elute later during the hold.

Refine near the best method with a slightly lower starting fraction and a modestly steeper gradient, aiming to bring the middle critical pair above 1.5 while retaining a last-peak time near 10 minutes. The final fraction remains above the observed elution window.

Test whether moving the persistent late co-elution into the final hold changes its selectivity enough to recover lost resolution credit. This exploratory run accepts a possible time penalty to assess a separation mechanism that the higher-ending gradients have not tested.

Refine around injection 8 with a slightly shallower slope and a small temperature increase to offset the added retention. This targets the marginal middle pair while keeping the last peak close to the 10-minute scoring boundary.

Explore a higher-start, shallower-gradient regime to test whether selectivity crossings can produce a better optimum than the current plateau. This risks compressing early peaks but should substantially change the middle-pair pattern while keeping late elution reasonably fast.

Test a substantially steeper gradient to look for a different selectivity optimum beyond the shallow-gradient plateau. The run should finish well below 10 minutes, allowing us to assess resolution without a time penalty.
Return to the best gradient and test a single 5-degree temperature step. This checks whether a modest selectivity shift improves the score while preserving the sub-10-minute last-peak time.

Test a slightly shallower slope than injection 8 to measure whether the remaining resolution gains justify crossing the 10-minute boundary. This brackets the local optimum rather than assuming the time penalty always outweighs improved separation.

Increase the endpoint one grid step from injection 11 to bring the last peak below 10 minutes. This tests whether the lower starting fraction preserves enough middle-pair resolution to outperform the current best without a time penalty.

Lengthen injection 7 by two minutes to improve its compressed middle pairs and late cluster while targeting a last peak just below 10 minutes. This tests the higher-start edge of the promising shallow-gradient region.

Test a slope between injections 7 and 8, with an endpoint above the expected last-peak elution fraction. This should eliminate injection 8’s small time penalty while retaining most of its resolution gains.

Test a lower-start gradient tuned to place the last peak near 10 minutes, between the initial broad gradient and the best narrowed window. This checks whether improved middle-pair separation can outweigh slightly weaker separation in the late cluster.

Apply a single temperature step to injection 8 to remove its small time penalty and directly test the local temperature tradeoff. The solvent window and slope remain unchanged so any score difference is attributable to temperature.

Test a shorter gradient ending near the last peak’s elution fraction, balancing hold-phase separation against the time penalty. This probes an untested endpoint near the best solvent window while retaining the favorable low temperature.

Refine between injections 11 and 18 with an intermediate slope, targeting full credit for the middle critical pairs with a smaller time penalty than injection 11. The endpoint should remain above the last peak’s elution fraction.

Use the final injection to test a slightly steeper neighbor of injection 8, aiming to remove its time penalty while preserving most of its critical-pair resolution. Retain 25 C, which consistently gave the strongest scores in this region.
